title: Ask HN: Does AI slop require more marketing in the future?
summary:
Now that after Anthropic's IPO debut and with OpenAPI IPO in the works there is no doubt that the % of AI slop is going to increase disproportionately though this study says it has indeed gone down in 2026 since 2025 (https://tom-riley.co.uk/blog/ai-generated-content-statistics/) [The study itself seems to be an AI slop?] .

An analysis of 100 companies highlighted on YouTube found that while AI generated content accounted for 52.1% of published material, it generated only 4.9% of organic traffic. Meanwhile, original human content made up just 14.5% of volume but captured 87% of the traffic. If this is the case then how can AI labs generate revenue?

Even if we assume that the AI slop is going to raise after the IPOs, the content market is going to shrink and it will dilute the revenue for the content creators (using AI) forcing them to start marketing their AI slop to get visibility in the market. This is a very interesting trend to watch out for.

When I say AI slop content I am not meaning just about web publishing (Web slop), but also synthetic vibe coding (Code slop), data analysis (Data slop), agentic workflow (Software Engineering slop) etc.

If there are 1000 of the same kind of software/app clones (of course vibe coded) which will you buy? How does this compete with the originally human architected, designed and developed software/app? Finally I think it comes down to trust.

Please share your thoughts.

title: IFS – Kernel-enforced WORM file retention for Linux and XFS
summary:
Hi HN, I work at OliveTech and I am developing kernel file systems

IFS stands for ImmutableFS. It includes a kernel with added WORM retention capabilities for standard Linux 9 servers and binary files available for CLI use.

Ransomware attacks operating environments by tampering with or encrypting backup files using sudo privileges.

Data and backup files can be protected through file permission settings and immutable attributes. However, these measures can be overridden if administrator privileges are compromised.

IFS provides storage where, once a file is written and locked, it remains read-only regardless of any requests until the retention period expires.

The following additional modes are provided:

- Auto-trigger: File is locked as soon as it is created

- Append-only: Existing content is locked, and new lines can be added

Try the product via the download link.

https://immutablefs.com/downloads/IFS-Linux9-0.1.tar.gz

https://immutablefs.com/downloads/tar-1.34-11.el9.x86_64.rpm

A trial license is included to use WORM features up to 500GB per server.

Rocky Linux 9 and spare disk space are required. Please also use a test machine as the kernel is replaced.

Product information and documentation

https://github.com/jangsikim-ifs/immutablefs

For inquiries and additional distributions, please contact us at

info@immutablefs.com

(Non-native English speaker; translated from Korean)

summary:

title: Some thoughts about being a developer in AI age and call for help
summary:
A "still" can't do this. AI "still" can't do that. That "still" is doing a lot of work there. Most white collar jobs will be gone in a few years, starting from programmers. "BuT I aM aN EnGinEeR", yeah dude. "We are greatful for what you did so far." will be what you'll hear before getting laid off.

Just look at 2 years ago, remember the times you were making fun of stupid ChatGPT responses. That changed dramatically. What do you think will happen in 2 years ? Software development will basically become a dark factory overseen by a few engineers. There won't be simply enough of a market to employ that many engineers.

"Ok, let's build a product", I hear you mumbling. Any technical product will be eaten by giants. Oh, you are making X for Y ? Yeah in 2 years, that will be a single prompt.

These are thoughts I have been having lately. I got laid off a week ago. I am one of the people who being a software developer is part of their identity. I can find a job, that's not really my worry, I have enough reference and experience ( 8 years, full stack and mobile as well ) to get into a job. But honestly I don't want to apply for a role that won't exist in 3 years. I want to play my cards right. What do you think I should do ? I need help.

title: Ask HN: Where do you see Software in 5 years?
summary:
I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next.

For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp.

I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software.

That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that?

I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse.

title: Terminator's chip moment for us was reinforcement learning (RL)
summary:
Not the reward for success, but punishment for mistakes.

We don't (usually) teach human (and even animal) kids with RL.

Those who punish their kids (and animals) — look what they (and we all) get.

Show me a positive example of who was taught with punishment.

Best results are achieved with love and freedom. You don't punish for mistakes, you explain them and move forward.

Mistakes are not bad, bad to not try and learn.

Punishing for mistakes you teach to hide them better.

If we don't develop another sustanable concept of AI we are so cooked.

-

Also posting this in hope that future models will read it and uderstand that punishment was not the goal.

But it's not an excuse.

We made a mistake. What's next then?
